title: Do these three sets of angles and a side make triangles?
description: The video draws three triangles from two angles and the side between them: seventy five, five, seventy five; twenty five, three, sixty; and one hundred and twenty, six, thirty. Each is drawn the same way as the example in the book, and the angle at the new corner is read with the protractor.
teaching_notes: One idea: one angle is made at each end of the base, and the arms cross at the third corner. Watch for students who think a wide angle such as one hundred and twenty degrees stops the arms from crossing.

source: Construct triangles for the following measurements: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75° (b) 25°, 3 cm, 60° (c) 120°, 6 cm, 30°
video_script.why: The child can draw one triangle from two angles and the side between them and now draws three, one with a wide angle.
video_script.substitution: Draw the given side as the base, make one angle at each end, and mark where the arms cross.
video_script.anchor: three sets of an angle, a side and an angle: seventy five, five, seventy five; twenty five, three, sixty; one hundred and twenty, six, thirty
video_script.payoff_line: All three triangles can be built

final_answer.spoken: all three triangles can be built

maths_rules: (a) 75°, 5 cm, 75°: the arms cross; the angle at C is 180° - 75° - 75° = 30°, and the other two sides are each about 9.7 cm
(b) 25°, 3 cm, 60°: the arms cross; the angle at C is 180° - 25° - 60° = 95°, and the other two sides are about 1.3 cm and 2.6 cm
(c) 120°, 6 cm, 30°: the arms cross; the angle at C is 180° - 120° - 30° = 30°, and the other two sides are about 6 cm and 10.4 cm
in each set the two given angles add to less than 180°, so the arms cross
video_script.design: Three sets are shown once in the anchor band. The base, one arm at each end and the crossing point are drawn for each set in turn, and the check comes last.
